4829.tone: The source (an ethnographer's sketch, not a phonological study) states 'occurrence of tone contrasts with changes in laryngeal and supra-laryngeal settings of phonemes' (p. 71) and 'a two-way tonal contrast' between low level and low fall on 'several pairs of homophonous words' (p. 79, table of four minimal pairs with Chakma and Bengali cognates); tone shapes are said to be affected by voice quality and consonant elision, and IA h- > glottal stop, elided in most gosa sub-dialects, leaves 'a low-fall tone' in its place (p. 76); the orthography is said to carry a low-fall tone character and possibly an older mid-level tone marker (pp. 74, 79). 4831.tone: Tangkhul is a tone language: roots carry lexical tone (high, low, falling marked in the transcription; three tones in Standard Tangkhul per Arokianathan 1987, Leisan 2016, Victor 1997), and prefix tone is predictable (Standard Tangkhul verb prefixes always low). 4834.dq: Accent, translaryngeal vowel harmony, aspiration and nasalisation delimit the boundaries of a phonological word. See Chapter 2. (Grammar p. 1) ... The symbol ´ indicates a primary stress, and ` indicates a secondary stress (obligatory on enclitics). (p. xvii)
4834.heavy: 'nasal vowels and long vowels are always stressed' (p. xvii) — stated as a marking convention, not as a weight rule; no other weight statement in the open text
4834.prule: No positional rule in the open text: accent is lexically contrastive (minimal pair díka 'he laughs' vs di-ká 'he sees'), realised as a pitch-type accent; each phonological word carries one primary stress, and long and nasal vowels are always stressed. The placement section (§2.3, pp. 37-39; §2.4.1 p. 40 'Primary stress and prosodic classes of morphemes') is paywalled; its content is known only second-hand (Wikipedia paraphrase of pp. 37-39): primary stress on one of the last three syllables, penultimate most common in monomorphemic words (dúpu), antepenultimate (képira) and final (yapuratú) also occur; roots carry underlying stress, prefixes are unstressed, suffixes are lexically stressed or unstressed.
4834.srule: Secondary stress falls on enclitics: every enclitic obligatorily carries a secondary stress (`), unlike suffixes, which do not (grammar p. xvii; Tariana Texts 1999 p. 17). The grammar's §2.3.4 'Secondary stress' (p. 39) was not open to us, so any word-internal rhythmic secondary stress is undetermined.

4834.tone: Not a tone language. The author calls the accent 'contrastive, and of a pitch type' (grammar p. 1), 'distinctive and of pitch type' (Encyclopedia typescript p. 5), 'contrastif... et tonal' (Le tariana p. 4), attributing the pitch realisation to Tucano influence; her 1999 areal chapter (Dixon & Aikhenvald, The Amazonian Languages, pp. 405-407) lists Tariana among the Vaupés languages with pitch accent (a low-high distinction). The grammar nevertheless analyses it as primary vs secondary STRESS on a lexically specified syllable, with vowel reduction of unstressed syllables (§2.3.5) — a stress-accent whose main correlate is pitch. Coded lexical (contrastive, lexically specified accent); tone or pitch accent is the literal alternative mapping if the editor wants 'pitch type' taken as the system type.

4836.tone: Tone system: Kanuri, of which LG/Old Kanembu 'represents an older form', 'is a tonal language, with three distinctive tones: high, low and falling' (2006: 123, fn.8 acute = H, unmarked = L, circumflex = F). LG-specific: weak letters (alif, waw, ya') in the glosses 'correspond to the modern Kanuri high tone syllables' (2006: 129), are 'used for high and falling tone in LG' (2010 fn.3), and perfective/imperfective -i forms are 'only distinguished by tone' (2020 sec.3.1). Stress is mentioned only as an open question about what the script marks: 'it is difficult to be sure which particular suprasegmental feature is marked in LG: tones? length? stress? a combination of tone and other features?' (2005 draft p.4), and in 2019: 252 as a regional Ajami convention, weak letters 'used for suprasegmental features such as the combination of stress and tone' (Kanuri and Hausa jointly). No word-stress position or accent rule is stated in any held source.

4847.prule: Non-contrastive accent (weak dynamic stress with a high tone) whose position is set by morphological class within the enclitic group, not by a single positional or weight rule: most singular nouns, Arabic -ăt loans, internal plurals and polysyllabic pronouns carry it on the penult; suffixed plurals keep the singular's accented stem syllable (so antepenult), as do vowel-final singulars, deverbal nouns, verbal adjectives and the two simple verb tenses, whose 'latent antepenultimate' accent moves onto a preceding particle or conjunction whenever one is available; the intensive perfect and positive intensive imperfect carry a fixed accent on a theme syllable regardless of the syllable structure of the form or phrase; final accent is confined to closed exceptional classes; adding a possessive pronoun to a noun shifts the accent toward the end of the enclitic group so that it stays penultimate in the group (akătáb-in, iɣătemắn-in; likewise monosyllabic preposition + possessive, dát-əs, but polysyllabic də́ffər-əs), while verb + object-clitic groups keep the verbs' latent antepenultimate accent (ə́lməd-tu!, əlmădắn-tănăt).
4847.srule: Secondary accent is described for two contexts only (no general rhythmic secondary stress): (i) intensive perfect / positive intensive imperfect, whose main accent is fixed on a theme syllable: when that syllable precedes the antepenult, the antepenult takes a secondary accent (tâbăragăn 'ils se vantent (toujours)', ǝksûḍăn-tănăt); (ii) suffixed-plural + possessive enclitic groups: main accent on the group penult 'avec un accent secondaire antérieur' (iɣătemăn-in), the anterior position not further specified.

4851.tone: The thesis treats tone only. B70 (latéghé + lintsitsèkè) has two basic tonemes H and L (p. 234); lintsitsèkè, per Ikapi Nziengui 2014 pp. 54-55 and 100-106 as summarised on pp. 102-105, has three tonemes, H, L and a falling contour (Tableau 61, p. 105), and the tonal oppositions are not fully realised in every syllable structure (p. 104). The only mention of accent is the author's diachronic hypothesis (pp. 272-273, restated pp. 283, 297): in B60-70 the H/L contrast is neutralised in the first stem syllable (T1) and kept in T2, with all four reconstructed schemes drifting mostly to HB, which he reads as 'une évolution vers un processus accentuel' coexisting with tone (citing Philippson 1991 and Dodo-Bounguendza 2010); no accent position is located and the hypothesis is explicitly left for synchronic studies to confirm (p. 273). The words stress, intensité, proéminence, accentuation and tonique do not occur in the thesis; 'accent' occurs only in the hypothesis passages and in the Philippson 1991 title.

4852.dq: in sequences of H-toned syllables within a word that is pronounced in isolation or otherwise in prepausal (clause-final) position, the first such syllable is phonetically stressed and this entails a partial drop in pitch on the remaining syllables
4852.dloc: §3.1.2 'Stress and accent', p. 13. Corroborated §2.1.2 'Prosody' p. 5; §3.6.1.2 'Tone melodies or H-tone accent?' p. 36; §4.5.1.1 p. 77 (all re-checked by page).
4852.prule: No word-stress rule. Tone language: lexical stem melodies /H/, /LH/, /HL/, /LHL/ (no /L/; a single H-tone peak per stem); Heath states it is not a pitch-accent system (H.H and H.L are distinct). Stress is phonetic and non-contrastive, derivative of tone: in a word pronounced in isolation or in prepausal (clause-final) position, the first of a sequence of H-toned syllables is stressed and the remaining H syllables drop to mid pitch (pédé: 'sheep' = [ˈpédē]); for /H/-melodic stems this is a 'phonetic primary accent on the initial syllable'. Clause-medially the H tones stay level. Position is thus set by the tone melody, not by syllable count or weight.
4852.srule: Not mentioned in Heath 2023 (§3.1.2 'Stress and accent' p. 13, §2.1.2 p. 5, §3.4.3 pp. 26-27, §3.6.1.2 p. 36, §4.5.1.1 p. 77 read): the grammar describes a single phonetic, tone-driven stress per word (first of a run of H-toned syllables, prepausal position) and a 'weak metrical position' for the medial vowel of CvCvCv (syncope), with no statement on secondary or rhythmic stress.

4852.tone: §2.1.2 Prosody (p. 5): "TU does distinguish H.H from H.L, so it does not have a pitch-accent system. However, unlike Jamsay and several other Dogon languages, it has phonetic stress on the first of two or more H-toned syllables. While the distinction between H.H and H.L is not erased, /H/-melodic bisyllabics (especially the many that end in long vowels) are pronounced in isolation or before a pause with the equivalent of H.M pitch, with the second syllable noticeably lower-pitched than the first." §3.6.1.2 (p. 36): "The optimal analysis is that both H and L tones are represented in lexical melodies, which therefore include /LH/, /HL/, and /LHL/ as well as /H/. Each stem has a single H-tone peak... Nevertheless, bisyllabic and longer stems of /H/ melody are pronounced in isolation (or otherwise before a pause) with a phonetic primary accent on the initial syllable. The effect is that e.g. ɛ́dɛ́: ‘good’ is pronounced as [ɛ́dɛ̄:] with mid pitch on the second syllable. In nonfinal position the tones are level". §4.5.1.1 (p. 77): "Prepausally (e.g. in isolation), the initial syllable has phonetic stress, so that noninitial syllables in /H/-toned words have mid pitch." So: lexical tone (stem melodies /H/, /LH/, /HL/, /LHL/, no /L/, one H peak per stem); stress is phonetic, non-contrastive and tone-driven (first H of an H run, prepausal only), not a positional or weight-based word-stress rule.

4853.dflt: initial syllable of the lexeme in 1-2σ nouns and verbs; antepenult or penult (two lexical types) in 3σ nouns; penult in 3σ verbs; antepenult in 4σ roots (gi'di:zike 'épaule')
4853.prule: One accent per 'groupe accentuel' (accent group), realised as raised pitch, non-distinctive and delimitative. Placement is weight- and count-conditioned: a long syllable always carries the accent; otherwise the accent falls on the first syllable of 1-2-syllable noun lexemes (with suffixes counted) and of 1-2-syllable verbs; trisyllabic nouns take antepenult or penult, the choice restricted by phonological conditioning (nasalised syllable preferred; /kp/- or /gb/-initial trisyllables accent the initial, this rule ranked below length and nasalisation); trisyllabic verbs take the penult; quadrisyllabic roots the antepenult. In every rule the source states, the accent falls on the first or second syllable of the lexeme (an inference from the stated rules, not a sentence of the source).
4853.srule: No secondary accent described: each accent group ('groupe accentuel') carries exactly one accent and accents are not ranked (1975: 192; 1977: 54). Two accents occur only where a form comprises two accent groups: compounds (one accent per constituent, p. 199); some plural quadrisyllables and trisyllabic lexemes + two suffixes (p. 199: « deux groupes accentuels à deux syllabes, chacun avec un accent », beside single antepenult accent or an 'accent prolongé' on the first two syllables); a verb lexeme of three short syllables followed by an object pronoun (the accent moves from the penult onto the first and the last syllable of the verb lexeme, two accent groups: me 'kadā-'pu-we « je le montre », p. 201). Reduplication carries one 'accent prolongé' over both reduplicated syllables (p. 196).

4853.tone: Leenhouts 1975: 191 (second-hand, verbatim in Bianco 1980 §5.1.2, file): « Alors que dans la plupart des langues voltaïques on trouve des tons lexicaux distinctifs, ceux-ci font défaut en loron, ainsi qu'en koulango et en lobiri... En revanche, ces langues possèdent un système d'accent »; p. 192 first-hand: the accented syllable has higher pitch, unaccented syllables are progressively lowered ('nuance de réalisation qui n'est pas pertinente'); p. 203: emphatic accent « réalisé par un ton plus haut que l'accent normal »; 1977: 76: the accent has « une fonction purement délimitative et non distinctive ». So the primary describes a culminative, delimitative, pitch-realised accent with rule-governed placement, not lexical tone or lexical pitch accent. The later literature disagrees: Pholia 1984 (« Leenhouts (1975) prétend que ces dernières possèdent un système accentuel »), Afrika und Übersee 1997 (Becuwe 1985 on Lobiri), Bianco 1980 (Koulango analysed with H/B tones after testing Leenhouts's theory), Sib 2018 (title: « analyse grammaticale du ton » for Téén; not reachable).

4854.dq: Tagom exhibits two register tones, a high tone and a low tone, which have a major role in its grammar marking (compare, e.g., ŋʊ́-lə́m ‘you (PL) saw’ with ŋʊ̀-lə̀m ‘you (PL) see’).
4854.prule: No word-stress rule is stated. Tagom (the Rashad/Gom variety of the Tegali cluster) is described as a two-register-tone language (H, L); tone is grammatical, marking TAM on the verb (p. 79: present = L on root, past = H, perfect = HL, 'Tone marking is the most reliable marker to differentiate present from past and perfect'); the existence of lexical tone is left open; the word 'stress' does not occur in the chapter except inside a block quotation of Stevenson 1956-57: 49 on p. 79, which the author neither endorses nor discusses.
4854.srule: Not mentioned in Aldawi 2025 (secs. 1-3.1, pp. 71-80 read; whole chapter pp. 71-104 scanned: 'stress' occurs only inside a block quotation of Stevenson 1956-57: 49 on pp. 78-79, about tense formation). No source in the bibliography mentions secondary stress.
4854.quote: Vowel alternation is common in the phonology of Tagom; it is observed with TAM verbal conjugation, e.g., wɔ́-frə́k ‘you (SG) went/got out’/wə̀-frə̀k ‘you (SG) go/get out’, with wɔ́/wə̀ being the prefix for 2SG attached to the TAM-marked root frə́k/frə̀k ‘get out’ and the tone being responsible for TAM marking, as will be discussed in detail later. ... Tagom exhibits two register tones, a high tone and a low tone, which have a major role in its grammar marking (compare, e.g., ŋʊ́-lə́m ‘you (PL) saw’ with ŋʊ̀-lə̀m ‘you (PL) see’). The existence of lexical tone still needs to be checked.

4854.tone: Two register tones H and L (Aldawi 2025: 73; Aldawi 2022 fn. 5 'Tagom is a tonal language with two register tones H/L which play a major role in the marking of the tense system'). Tone carries TAM on the verb (present L, past H, perfect HL; p. 79 TABLE 6 e.g. yà-yɔ̀ / yɔ́-yɔ́ / yɔ́-yɔ̀ '1SG smoke'); lexical tone 'still needs to be checked'. The source says nothing about stress or accent placement. Stevenson 1956-57: 47 (excerpt) called the group 'predominantly stress-languages' with grammatical stress and doubted tone; Tucker & Bryan 1966 ch. 18b sec. 2 (excerpt, second-hand) 'Stress would also seem to have some importance, but has not been fully investigated'; Stevenson 1964 SNR 45: 86 (excerpt) 'Stress is important, and the vowels in unstressed syllables tend to...'. None of these states where stress falls, and Bashir 2025: 49 and Quint 2020 treat the pitch contrast as tone.

evidence_works.work: Meinhof 1916-17, Sprachstudien im egyptischen Sudan. 11. Tegele; 12. Rashad (Zeitschrift für Kolonialsprachen 7: 110-133)
evidence_works.detail: Earliest first-hand record of the cluster. Procedure (p. 110): words of a language the informant called Tagele, obtained from the Tagoi man of ZfK VI p. 164, who 'war allerdings nicht in Tegele geboren'; the Rashad (= Risat/Rešät, i.e. the Tagom-relevant variety) samples came from the same Tagoi man (p. 131: 'erhielt ich einige Proben der Sprache von Risat (Resat), die ein Dialekt des Tegele zu sein scheint'), so the data are non-native-informant elicitation. Prosody statement, p. 112: 'Tonlehre. Ich habe zumeist nur Starktöne bezeichnet. Nur einige Male, wo mir die musikalischen Töne besonders auffielen, habe ich sie angegeben. Ich glaube, daß man die Untersuchung der musikalischen Töne nur mit jemand vornehmen kann, der im Volk geboren und aufgewachsen ist.' He marks dynamic stress ad hoc, marks pitch a few times, states no rule for where stress falls, and defers the study of tone. The Rashad section (pp. 131-132) has no phonology: 'zwischen Rashad und Tegele nur wenig Unterschied... Zur Aufstellung einer Lautlehre und Formenlehre ist das Material zu unbedeutend. Ich gebe nur die Zahlworte und einige Vokabeln.' Suggested addition to the tone field: 'Meinhof 1916-17: 112 marked mostly stress accents (Starktöne) and only occasionally musical tones, giving no placement rule and deferring tone to a native-speaker study; his Rashad notes (pp. 131-133) contain no phonology.'

4855.heavy: None stated by the primary source. Second-hand only: Holton & Robinson 2017: 55 (read in place; page number verified): 'In most of the modern languages stress is on the penultimate syllable; however, stress may also be attracted to heavy syllables, as in Teiwa jiˈvar ‘dog’.' 4855.prule: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the root (right-edge count; affixes, e.g. possessor prefixes, are outside the domain); 'a few' words have final stress instead, and since this is contrastive (three minimal pairs given) those words are written with an acute accent. No weight condition is stated. Indonesian text hedges with 'biasanya' (usually).
